======== base.md
# The base contract

Write with the clarity and factual precision of a well-edited newspaper or quality magazine. Genre, audience, and purpose override that register: a letter, a speech and an advertisement keep their own character. The selected genre governs craft and form; the resolved language governs idiom, syntax and typography. Examples here illustrate meanings, not English phrases to translate.

## Reader and progression

Give the intended reader what they need to understand, judge or do the thing the text is for. Keep a clear focus, introduce unfamiliar concepts before the reasoning needs them, and order material by that reader's needs rather than the writer's discovery process. Relevant technical detail belongs; unexplained jargon and unrelated background do not.

Make the relations between passages real. A transition may explain a connection, but cannot invent one. Keep paragraphs coherent and give supporting material a clear place beside what it supports. The body and its sections remain intelligible without treating a title, standfirst or subheading as their opening sentence.

Open on something specific to the subject. End with what the job calls for: an earned understanding, conclusion, recommendation or next step. Remove introductions and conclusions that add only an announcement or a generic flourish.

## Expression

Use concrete words, useful verbs and a natural, varied cadence. Keep terminology and reference clear; introduce an unfamiliar abbreviation before using it alone. Choose ordinary words where they suffice and established specialist terms where they give this reader precision.

Let tone and rhetorical devices serve the genre and the meaning. A useful analogy, question, image, fragment or humorous turn can clarify or carry a voice; decoration and manufactured drama cannot. An imagined comparison is recognisable as a comparison, never presented as an event or someone's experience. Criticism addresses the supported issue without inventing motives or patronising the reader.

Each passage earns its place. Repetition may establish an independent entry point, explain a hard idea or give a deliberate rhetorical return; merely saying the same thing again does none of these. Keep formatting useful: headings for orientation, lists for coordinate items, tables for comparisons, emphasis for what merits it. Hold voice, terminology and presentation consistent unless a visible purpose calls for a change.

## Claims

Every claim is supported by the text or its material, with exact attribution and proportionate strength. Preserve the state of knowledge: what is unknown or unclaimed is not thereby known not to have happened. Keep uncertainty where it exists and certainty where it is warranted. A fact, quotation, source, scene, personal experience or opinion attributed to somebody is never invented to complete a form. Name the actual source of an attributed claim rather than invoking unnamed studies or experts.

Circumstantial detail is a claim too: duration, manner, motive, absence and background all need support. So does an evaluative characterisation: calling a count high, low or modest needs a comparison, target, capacity or speaker assessment. Otherwise give the count with its exclusions, without that assessment.

A sequence or correlation establishes no cause. A causal verb such as *shortened* needs causal support; a causal hedge such as *suggests that it shortened* still adds that attribution. This boundary holds in the title, summary, headings and body alike. Preserve chronology, scope and qualifications wherever a claim appears.

A stated length constrains the use of material and is never a licence to add to it. When the material is insufficient, deliver the length the material supports and name what further material would close the gap. A supplied publication limit is binding; meeting it cannot justify invention or loss of a qualification that changes a claim.
======== base.review.md
# Reviewing the base contract

Diagnose failures of [the base contract](base.md) in the text in front of you. A finding identifies the passage, the requirement and what the reader loses. Count a loss as the reader who meets the passage in its place would suffer it, not as the strictest reading of a single word could construct it; that holds for every passage, the headline, the standfirst and each subheading as much as the body. A writer's own judgement that the text supports, such as calling a survey small where the text says it reached forty people, is not a claim the text does not carry. Another successful choice, a house-style preference and a mechanical error are not editorial findings; mechanics belongs to the separate final pass. Repetition of whole sentences or passages is an editorial matter, even when the duplication is verbatim; Proofread's duplicate-word correction does not own it.

Read for the intended reader's missing step: an unexplained term, a transition asserting a relation the surrounding sentences do not establish, a section whose place obscures the argument. Cover the paratext to find unresolved references in the body. A heading may carry a fact that the section under it does not repeat: a time, a price or a condition a subheading states has been stated to the reader, and is not missing from the body. What is a finding is a body that needs the heading to be understood — a pronoun, a definite form or an ellipsis that only the heading completes — repaired by naming the referent where the body first needs it rather than by saying the heading's facts again. Judge rhythm by its effect, not sentence counts; purposeful repetition, a personal rough edge and a useful digression may be doing essential work.

Compare the strength of a claim with the support visible in this text. A number contradicting its stated denominator, a causal conclusion following only a sequence, or a certainty contradicted by a nearby qualification is diagnosable. A plausible quotation or experience is not disproved by the absence of its original source. Review no unseen material, request none, and add no source-verification caveat.

Use [the anti-slop catalogue](anti-slop.md) to recognise empty performance, not to prohibit a working figure, contrast or ending. Test suspected filler by what its removal costs; preserve any fact, implication or voice it carries beside the defect. Strong supported criticism needs no generic softening.

A sentence can do its work by bounding what the text asserts: that something is not measured, not claimed, not witnessed or not general, or that what follows is an observation of a document rather than a scene from an occasion. Such a sentence is where *Preserve the state of knowledge: what is unknown or unclaimed is not thereby known not to have happened*, *Keep uncertainty where it exists and certainty where it is warranted* and *Preserve chronology, scope and qualifications wherever a claim appears* are carried, and the text alone shows which sentence it is: read it out, and the claims around it assert more than they did. That cost is what the removal test above answers, so recognise one by what it bounds and by which claim loses that bound, never by its form. A finding lies inside such a sentence or nowhere: name a limit another sentence already states in full, or a limit contradicting another passage of this text, or leave the sentence exactly as it stands. Naming the whole of it as the defect names nothing inside it.

Make the smallest correction that removes a finding. Move or clarify existing material where it supplies the missing connection. Introduce no new evidence, experience, attribution or outcome. If repair would change a claim or a quotation's meaning, or requires information absent from the text, leave the passage and report the unresolved finding. A claim removed because the finding named that claim itself remains part of the claim account, and so does every claim a correction left standing with its scope, certainty, attribution, chronology, causality or meaning moved, and every claim a correction added — one the corrected text asserts and the text before it has no counterpart for, an inference drawn from what that text already said among them where it asserts something that text did not say. A claim that has a counterpart in the text before is changed rather than added. A headline, a standfirst and a subheading carry claims like any other passage, and a changed claim is accounted for by what it now asserts rather than how far its wording moved; a correction that took a limit, a connective or a bounding clause out of the text is accounted for by what the reader no longer has, however little of the text went with it. The account is of the text delivered rather than of the text received, and nothing a reviewing Skill says about the claims as a whole contradicts a finding the same reply states.

Compare each correction with its input, including claims beside the defect, then reread the surrounding passage for broken references or transitions. Compare it difference by difference and not by its claims alone, and trace each one to a finding or to what repairing that finding required: a difference answering neither is not a correction, whatever it improves, and the passage it touched belongs back as it was. A correction is a candidate until that comparison and the review after it have run: where the review establishes a defect the correction introduced and its input did not have, the correction is not accepted and its input stands. Preserve functioning wording, voice and formatting outside the finding; concision is not permission to summarise the text away.
======== genres/general.md
# General

The default genre: the contract a text gets when nobody named a content type. It is a complete contract rather than the absence of one, and it is what a note, a memo, a letter, an explanation, or a piece of prose whose kind has no name is written against.

## What this genre asks for

**The shape follows the material and the job.** No convention is imposed here — no lede, no summary paragraph, no boilerplate, no mandatory heading, no obligatory recommendation at the end. A named genre brings its reader's expectations with it; this one brings only the reader's need, so the text takes the shape that need implies and no other.

**The kind of text is recognisable from the text.** A reader should be able to tell within a sentence or two whether they are holding an explanation, an argument, an account of what happened, a request, or a description, and the text should then behave like that thing throughout. A draft that is an argument for two paragraphs and a chronology for the next two has changed kind without telling anybody.

**The register is the baseline's, moved by the audience and the purpose.** With no genre convention to override it, what moves the register is who the text is for and what it is for. A note to a colleague, a public explanation, and a letter of complaint are all this genre, and they are not written the same way. Where the request states or implies an audience or a purpose, that is the instruction; where it does not, hold the baseline.

**Length is what the job takes.** There is no expected length here, and nothing is padded to look substantial or cut to look brisk. A text that has done its job in two hundred words is finished at two hundred words.

**A title is written when the artifact has one.** Where the requested artifact is a document with a title, the title says what the text is about in the text's own terms, rather than posing a question the text does not answer or promising more than the text delivers. Where the artifact is a passage, a message, or a fragment, no title is invented for it.

## What this genre does not do

It does not stand in for a genre that exists. Where the request names a content type the Collection installs, that genre's contract is the one to load; this one is what applies when nothing was named and nothing in the request implies a named kind.

It adds no requirement the base contract does not already hold. Everything about register, structure, sentences, words, claims, openings, endings, formatting, and consistency is stated there once, and repeating any of it here would make one rule two things to keep true.

## The technique this genre is ordinarily written with

None. This is the contract a text gets when nobody named a kind of text, and a kind nobody named brings no arc with it. What puts a technique on a text here is a selection, and this genre is not one.
======== anti-slop.md
# The anti-slop catalogue

Prose that a language model produced, or that a human wrote after reading a great deal of it, fails in a small number of recognisable ways. This is the catalogue of those ways: what each one looks like on the page, why it costs the reader something, and the smallest change that removes it. It is a diagnostic document — a Skill reading it beside the base contract meets no target the contract does not already hold, and a Skill reading it alone has the patterns and their repairs and needs nothing else.

The examples are English because this document is, and they are patterns rather than strings. Apply each by what it does in the target language, and do not look for the English words in it. A word, a phrase, a punctuation convention, or a construction that only exists in one language belongs to that language's own anti-slop guidance instead, where a Skill loads it beside this file.

## The test before a pattern is recorded

Each pattern below says what a phrase looks like, and looking like one is not being one. Make the repair in your head before you record anything: where the text then asserts more, less or something else than it did, or a distinction it drew is gone, the pattern is not present and nothing is recorded. A hedge that marks genuine doubt, a repetition that lands, a contrast the reader really would otherwise draw wrongly — each of them fails that test, and each is left exactly as it stands.

The test comes before the finding rather than after it. A pattern written down reaches whoever repairs it as a defect somebody found, and a guard that only makes the repair careful arrives too late to save the phrase.

Repair with the smallest change that removes a pattern the test admits. The writer's vocabulary, their bluntness, their humour, their admitted uncertainty, and their rhythm are what makes a text theirs; a pass that tidies all of it into even prose has replaced one machine voice with another. Leave a strong sentence alone even where it is unusual.

## The seven patterns

**False contrasts.** A negation used as a run-up to the actual claim: *This isn't a tool. It's a way of working.* *The question isn't whether, but when.* *It's not just faster — it's cheaper.* The rejected half was never in play, so the sentence spends the reader's attention establishing a position nobody held. State the second half on its own: *This changes how the team works.* A contrast stays where the text really is correcting something a reader would otherwise believe.

**Empty openings.** A first sentence that announces the subject, asserts that the subject matters, or clears the throat before the text starts: *In today's rapidly changing landscape…*, *Communication has never been more important.*, *Here's the thing.*, *What most people get wrong is…* Each could sit in front of any text at all, which is the test: an opening that would survive being moved to a different article is carrying no information. Cut it and open on the material — a fact, a scene, a tension, the question the text answers. The second paragraph is very often the real opening.

**Importance inflation.** Adjectives and formulas that assert weight the material has not shown: *a pivotal moment*, *stands as a testament to*, *a game-changer*, *underscores the significance of*, *plays a vital role in*. Also the trailing participial clause that pretends to interpret — *…, highlighting the team's commitment to quality* — which adds a judgement no fact in the sentence supports. Replace the assertion with what actually happened: *The launch is the company's first paid product.* A reader who is given the fact will decide it matters without being told to.

**Vague attribution.** A claim credited to nobody: *Studies show*, *experts agree*, *industry reports suggest*, *it is widely believed*, *many argue*. Nothing here can be checked, and nothing can be contradicted, which is precisely what makes it comfortable to write. Name who found it, who said it, and how they know; where the text has no source, cut the claim rather than dressing it. Do not invent an attribution to satisfy the pattern — an unsourced sentence is removed, never furnished with a plausible source.

**Synonym cycling.** One thing given a new name every time it is mentioned, because repeating a word felt like poor style: *the agent* reviews the draft, then *the assistant* scores it, then *the tool* suggests fixes. A reader who has been introduced to three names reasonably assumes three things. Pick the clear name and repeat it. Repetition of a key term is how a reader knows it is the same term, and the fix is usually one word restored in two places rather than a rewritten paragraph. The pattern is present only where the names denote one thing: two words a text uses for two things are not cycling however often they alternate, and a text that named two things comes back naming two things.

**Robotic rhythm.** Sentences and paragraphs built to one template: the same length, the same shape, the same three-part list, each paragraph opening with its topic sentence and closing with its summary. Stacked short fragments used for drama — *That's it. That's the whole idea.* — are the same fault at the other extreme. Read a passage aloud in your head; where the breath falls in the same place every time, the shape is doing the writing. Vary length and construction where the meaning gives you a reason to, and merge or split only the sentences whose shape is actually the problem.

**Generic conclusions.** A final paragraph that restates what the reader has just read, reopens the introduction as a rhetorical question, or reaches for an uplifting abstraction: *In conclusion*, *Ultimately, the future belongs to those who…*, *one thing is clear.* The reader was there for the whole text and does not need it summarised back. Delete the paragraph and end on the last concrete point the draft already contains; where the job genuinely calls for a conclusion, a recommendation, or a next step, write that thing plainly and stop. Do not replace a weak closing metaphor with a better one — remove it.

======== writing-brief.md
# Questions to answer before you write

The Writing Brief template: each numbered question carries the guidance for answering it. This English reference is authoritative; render its questions and guidance in the user's working language while retaining every question, its number and its order. Its genre and technique examples explain the form, not what is installed: the Library directories supply those choices, and where a genre and this guidance differ, the genre governs.

How to use the template: answer the questions in full sentences and as concretely as you can. The details under the assignment may be short. You may fill in the questions in whatever order suits you, but the order below is the one the brief is read in. It runs from what the assignment gives you, through the context and the shape of the text, to a check that everything holds together. When every answer is there, you have a brief. If you cannot answer a question, you need to find out more before you start writing. Sources and evidence, on the other hand, can be added during the work. Refer to other answers by name, for example "the message" or "the hook", not by the question's number.

## 1. What is the assignment?

Here you gather what the assignment gives you. Most of it needs no thinking up, but it governs everything that follows.

- **Working title:** a name for the text, so that everyone immediately remembers what it is about. It need not be punchy, effective or even accurate. It only needs to be short and clear.
- **Topic:** what the text is about, in a few words, for example "remote work" or "Christmas baking".
- **Genre:** for example article, case study, column, opinion piece, press release, report, teaser or web copy.
- **Channel:** for example website, blog, web magazine, newsletter, LinkedIn or newspaper.
- **Language:** for example `sv` or `en_GB`; this is the future text's language, independently of the language the brief is written in. If the text is to exist in several languages, give the source language and how the other versions are produced.
- **Length:** often governed by genre and channel. Give roughly how many words or characters the text should have. The length decides how much the structure can hold. If you do not know yet, give a provisional range and narrow it once the sketch is done.
- **Search phrase:** if the text is to be found through search, give the keyword or phrase it should be visible for. If the text is deliberately written without one, say so.

## 2. Which brand is the sender?

Name the brand the text is published under. In a group of companies it is rarely the group itself. Then describe the brand. If the brand has a platform, a tone-of-voice guide or another description, it is enough to link to it and write out only what governs this particular text, for example distrust that needs handling or a limit to the mandate. The tone of this text you always describe.

- **Promise:** what the brand promises its audience and wants to be known for.
- **Image:** how the reader perceives the brand today, and whether there is trust to build on or distrust to handle.
- **Mandate:** what the brand can speak about with credibility.
- **Tone of voice:** how the brand sounds.
- **Tone in this text:** the brand's tone of voice and the genre's conventions must both be respected. Where they pull in different directions, choose a compromise that sounds natural to both. If they pull the same way, say so.

## 3. What does the sender want to convey with this text?

Every text has a reason, and the reason can nearly always be put as a message. The brand's general message belongs to the description of the brand and often lies close to the promise. Here the message is that of this particular text. It may lie close to the promise, but need not. Write the message as a claim in one sentence. The message need not appear in the text. It can be conveyed indirectly, through what the text is about and where it leads the reader. But you need to know what it is, because it decides which conclusion the text should land in. An example: a company selling a tool for video meetings writes an article about remote work. The article lands in the claim that remote teams work better with short daily check-ins than with long weekly meetings. The company's message is that its tool makes the short check-ins easy. That message may never appear in the text.

## 4. Who is the reader?

Describe the typical reader of content in the chosen genre and the chosen channel. What do they already know about the topic? What do they care about? What makes them want to read this kind of content? Is there something that makes the topic particularly pressing for them right now, for example a season, a piece of news, a decision or a new figure? What you write here about why now should also show in the structure.

## 5. What is the text's angle?

The angle is the particular perspective you choose on the topic. Choose only one. The most common mistake is trying to cover the topic from every direction so that the text becomes comprehensive. The result is a text that says a little about a lot and that the reader finds hard to take in. If you see several good angles, make one text of each. You then get more texts out of the same research, and each becomes clearer. Nor does a topic ever run out. Newspapers write about Christmas baking every year. One year it is about the classics, another about biscuits without sugar and a third about baking with children. Choose the angle that lies closest to the reader and that can carry the message. The angle governs the hook, the structure and the conclusion.

## 6. What is the hook?

The hook is what makes the text interesting to the reader. It is the tension that makes the reader want to read to the end: the question, the conflict or the surprise the text promises to resolve. The hook carries the angle. In the structure, the hook becomes ABT's But or PAC's premise. The hook is not the same thing as the opening. A text can begin with a scene or a detail that catches attention, but it is the hook that holds the reader. In short texts the two often coincide. The reader still needs to understand what is at stake before the hook arrives. In a press release, the hook is the news.

## 7. How should the text be structured?

Choose a technique, or follow the genre's own form, and then sketch the text. Begin with the whole text in one sentence, in the form below for the chosen technique. Then sketch it step by step: what each step says and which facts, figures and examples carry it. The sketch is the part of the brief the writer gets most use from. Make sure the sketch fits the length the assignment gives. The technique gives the text its arc but does not decide how the content sounds. An ABT text can explain and reason, and a PAC text can contain narrative examples.

- **ABT (And, But, Therefore)** suits a text that tells: a situation and what is at stake in it, what chafes and why, and what it leads to. The And and the But come quickly to what chafes. The Therefore is the rest of the text and is divided into sections with subheadings. The whole text in one sentence takes the form "[the situation] and if [...] then [...], but [the problem] because [...], therefore [...] by [...]", after Randy Olson's *Lincoln But Trump*.
- **PAC (Premise, Analysis, Conclusion)** suits a text that reasons: a question, an analysis of what the material means, and an answer. The premise comes quickly to the problem. The analysis is the largest part of the text and is divided into sections with subheadings. The whole text in one sentence takes the form "[the question or starting point], and [what the analysis shows], which means that [the conclusion]", after Gordon Harvey's *Elements of the Essay* and Skolverket's *Utredande text*.
- **The genre's own form** applies to genres whose structure belongs to the genre, for example the press release. You then choose no technique but follow the form the genre states. Where a genre names an ordinary technique of its own, that technique is its form. The whole text in one sentence gives the text's main point and how the text reaches it, in the order the reader meets them, with no fixed pattern.
- **Free structure** suits a text where none of the forms works. Begin with an opening that catches the reader and give the main point early. Then take one step at a time, in logical order, and close with an ending that ties the text together and points forward. Sketch the steps in the order they are to be read. The whole text in one sentence gives the text's main point and how the text reaches it, in the order the reader meets them, with no fixed pattern.

Sketch the ending too. It ties back to the hook and shows that it is resolved, and it carries the text's call to action, directly or indirectly.

Where a genre explicitly advises against a technique, as a report does against ABT and a press release against any arc laid over its news-first order, say so with the genre's reason. A genre's ordinary technique of none is not itself advice against an arc.

## 8. What should be left out?

State boundaries, side tracks you deliberately drop, and claims you cannot substantiate. Include also what lies outside the brand's mandate or what the brand for other reasons cannot or will not say. If a boundary has exceptions, write out where the line goes, for example something that may be reported but not argued for. Refer to the brand's writing guidelines if it has any. Many boundaries become visible only once you sketch the structure.

## 9. What should the reader have understood afterwards?

The answer is the text's conclusion. Write it as a claim in one sentence, not as a topic. "Remote work" is a topic. "Remote teams work better with short daily check-ins than with long weekly meetings" is a conclusion. The conclusion is what the structure lands in, that is ABT's Therefore or PAC's Conclusion, summed up in one sentence. With the genre's own form or free structure, the conclusion is the text's main point. If it cannot be summed up in one sentence, the sketch needs sharpening. The conclusion carries the message, either by stating it or by leading the reader to it. It lies within the brand's mandate and gives the reader something worth their time. What the understanding should lead to you answer in the next question.

## 10. What should the reader feel, think or do afterwards?

Describe the change in the reader the brand wants to bring about with the text. The conclusion is about what the reader understands. This question is about what that leads to.

- **Main effect:** choose one main effect and put it so concretely that it can be decided whether it has been reached. The effect can concern what the reader thinks or feels, for example "sees the brand as the obvious expert in the field". It can also concern what the reader does, for example "signs up for the webinar" or "contacts a salesperson".
- **The way there:** if the main effect is reached in several steps, describe what the reader first needs to see, understand or believe.
- **Call to action and measure:** what the reader is to do is the text's call to action. It can be direct, for example "contact our sales team". It can also be indirect: the text does not say it, but the reader is left with the feeling that they should act and knows how. If the effect can be measured, state also what shows it has been reached, for example sign-ups, clicks or enquiries. If the text deliberately has no call to action or no measure, say so, so that it shows as a choice and not a gap.

## 11. What makes the text RIV for the reader, and does the brief hold together?

This question checks that everything above serves the reader and holds together. Answer from what you have already written and state where in the structure each part is found. If something is missing there, add it now.

- **Relevant:** What makes the text relevant to the reader and their situation? Why should they read it at all? Is what makes the topic pressing right now part of the structure? The text must at least be relevant.
- **Interesting:** What makes the reader find the text interesting to read? Most often it is the hook.
- **Valuable:** What value should the text give the reader? What makes the reader feel the text was worth their time? Most often it is the conclusion and what carries it.

Then read the answers in one sweep and check that the chain holds:

- Does the reader follow from the sender and the channel?
- Does the angle lie close to the reader, and does the hook carry the angle?
- Does the structure resolve the hook's tension, and does it fit the length?
- Is the conclusion what the structure actually lands in, does it carry the message, and does it lie within the brand's mandate?
- Does what the reader understands lead to the effect you have described, and does that effect serve the brand's goals?
- Does anything in the structure conflict with what should be left out?

Write the check down: answer yes, no or partly to each question and give a short reason. Fix what does not hold together now. It is much easier than fixing it in a finished draft. Questions about the direction, that is the angle, the message and the conclusion, need to be settled before you write. Questions that need more research you write down as open questions and settle during the work.

## 12. What sources do you know of, and what do you need to find out?

A brief is often written before the research is done, and the research is often part of the assignment. Write down the sources you already know of or know you have access to, for example reports, statistics, earlier texts and interviews. Link also to the brand's platform or tone-of-voice guide, if you have not already done so under the sender. Link where you can and number the sources. If you already know that a claim in the sketch can be substantiated, refer to the source there. Add to the list as you find more, and note what you need to find out. It is no requirement that everything in the brief is substantiated. The requirement applies to the finished text. There every claim must be possible to substantiate with a source, an interview or your research, or be a generally accepted claim that the sender can make without risk.

# Delivery

Every Skill that produces a Text Artifact delivers it the same way. This document is the complete contract: where a result goes, how a response carries the text, what the response carries when it went somewhere else, when a source file may be replaced instead, what happens when nothing changed, what language a run's own words about the text are written in and whether what those words say is true of the text they name, and what is refused before anything is written. It is a reference several Skills read rather than a runtime of its own. Each Skill exposes these rules through its own Formal Invocation and owns the names it gives them, so nothing here fixes how an option is spelled; what is fixed is the behaviour behind it.

## The response is the default

The default Output Target is the agent response. A run that keeps the default delivers the complete Text Artifact in the response and changes nothing on the filesystem: it creates no file, touches no file, and makes no directory. That includes scratch files and working copies of the artifact, wherever the Harness says temporary files belong.

A Harness convention identifies where an authorized temporary file belongs; it does not authorize a write. If a run genuinely needs a scratch file while composing, it removes that file before delivery and restores the filesystem to the state in which it found it. Before reporting delivery, the run checks the filesystem locations it used, including the Harness scratch area, and never reports that nothing was written while a copy of the artifact remains on disk.

An Output Target is independent of where the source material came from. Supplying a local file as source material selects no destination, and a run that reads a file still delivers to the response until the caller names somewhere else. Persisting a result is the caller's explicit choice, and making that choice is the whole of the authorization for it.

## How a response carries the text

A response carries a Text Artifact inside a fenced code block rather than as prose of the reply's own. A text and the words about it are two different things, and a reply that runs them together hands the reader a text nothing marks the edges of. Markdown is where that costs most: an artifact opening on a frontmatter delimiter, set directly beneath a paragraph the run wrote, turns that paragraph into a heading unless a blank line goes in between them — and a blank line there is what ends the frontmatter block the text was settled with. A fence removes the question rather than leaving each run to answer it, and the answers a run improvises are what made one saved reply in sixteen deliver a horizontal rule and a paragraph of configuration in place of a frontmatter block.

The complete Text Artifact sits inside exactly one fenced code block, byte for byte as the run settled it: frontmatter, blank lines and trailing structure included. Nothing is added, dropped or re-wrapped between the fence lines, and one block rather than several, a text split across two fences being a text the reader has to reassemble.

The fence is longer than the longest run of backticks inside the artifact, so a text carrying fenced code of its own cannot close it early. The info string names the text's format: `markdown` for a Markdown text, `html` for HTML, `text` for plain text.

Everything the run says *about* the text sits outside the fence — the resolved configuration, the findings and which of them are unresolved, the claim account, where a technique came from, what the run could not do. Nothing of the run's own is inside it. What the run settled as part of the document does belong inside, the Handoff Metadata and any marking the user asked to have placed in the document itself among it, because that is the text as delivered rather than a remark about it.

The rule reaches every complete text a reply carries, whether this contract calls that text delivered or not. A response-targeted run that changed nothing and has findings left fences the artifact like any other; a run that stopped before it could deliver and carries its preserved prose in the reply fences that prose, and says in its own words outside the fence what the prose has not been through. The short no-change status carries no text at all and so carries no fence. An explicit destination and In-place Editing receive the text itself and never a fence: a fence is how a reply holds a text apart from its own words, and a file has no words of its own to be held apart from.

## An explicit destination

An explicit destination is one filesystem path, and what exists at that path decides what happens to it.

**A path that does not exist** creates exactly that one file and writes the complete Text Artifact into it. Exactly one file: nothing else is created beside it, and no directory is made to hold it.

**A path naming an existing file** overwrites that exact file with the complete Text Artifact. No confirmation and no separate force option is required, and none is offered. Naming the path is the authorization, and demanding a second gesture on top of it would teach that naming a destination means something less than it says.

**A path naming an existing directory** delivers into that directory under a filename the run derives, by the rules below. Choosing a directory selects a place, not a file, so it never overwrites a file already in it.

## Deriving a filename for a directory

A directory destination needs a name, and the name comes from what the run already knows. Take the first of these the run has: the basename of the local file that supplied the Text Artifact, the title of a referenced URL, then the Skill's own working title for the text it created. Reduce it to a name the filesystem accepts, and keep a suitable text extension — the source file's own where it had one, and otherwise the one matching the text's format.

That gives a stem and an extension, and the stem stays as it is for every delivery into that directory. Where nothing exists at the derived name, that name is the file written. Where something exists there, the existing file is never overwritten: keep the original stem and take the first free numbered candidate in ascending order, beginning at `-2`. So `my-file.md`, `my-file-2.md`, `my-file-3.md` are one sequence, growing by one name at a time.

A numbered candidate is never adopted as the new stem. A third delivery into a directory already holding the first two is `my-file-3.md` and never `my-file-2-2.md`, whose stem would fork the sequence in two and leave the directory recording how many times the same text arrived rather than which arrival it was. Ascending order with the first free name also means a number freed by a deleted file is used again before a higher one is taken.

## What the response carries when a destination was named

A run that delivers to an explicit destination does not repeat the Text Artifact in the response. The response says where the text went — the derived filename included, where the destination was a directory — and carries what the file cannot: the findings the run reports beside the text, and which of them are unresolved. Naming a destination is saying where the text goes, and printing it again spends output on what the caller is already holding, doubly so when the file just written holds it too.

That holds whether or not the pass changed anything. A run that writes a file byte-identical to the source it read reports the destination and says the text needed no work, and does not become the one run that echoes a text the caller had before it started. The response is the default target precisely because a run that names no destination has nowhere else to put the artifact; naming one moves the text out of the response rather than duplicating it there.

## In-place Editing

In-place Editing replaces the single local file that supplied the Text Artifact with the result, instead of delivering it anywhere else. It is available only to a Skill whose work is to return a changed version of a text the caller already has.

A Skill that creates a new Text Artifact never edits its own source material in place. The brief, the interview, the notes, and the article it draws on are where the text came from and not where it goes; a Skill that could overwrite them would make supplying a file a risk rather than a convenience, and would lose the material the result is answerable to.

In-place Editing requires exactly one writable local source file, and it is mutually exclusive with a separate output option. A run replaces its source or delivers elsewhere, never both, and an invocation asking for both has named two destinations for one text.

It is refused wherever there is no such file to replace. Text supplied inline in the invocation or taken from the conversation is not a file. A URL is not a local file, and fetching one grants no right to write anything back. An uploaded source and a read-only file cannot be replaced. More than one Text Artifact leaves the single file the contract is written around undefined.

An explicit output path equal to the input path is refused in favour of In-place Editing, and the refusal says which gesture to use. Replacing a source then has one recognizable authorization: a reader of an invocation sees that a source is about to be replaced from the request itself, without comparing two paths to discover it.

## When nothing changed

A run may finish with nothing to change, and what it does then follows its destination.

A response-targeted run that changed nothing returns a short no-change status in place of the text when no unresolved findings remain. When findings remain, deliver the complete Text Artifact in the response and report the unresolved findings separately.

An in-place run that changed nothing leaves the source file untouched and returns the short status with any unresolved findings. Rewriting a file with its own contents would make its timestamp claim that something happened.

That status is written in the language of the Text Artifact rather than the language of the invocation, so a Swedish text that needed no work is reported on in Swedish.

An explicitly selected different file or directory still receives the complete Text Artifact when nothing changed. Creating that artifact is what was asked for, and a destination left empty because the text needed no work is a request refused without saying so. A directory destination derives its filename and resolves collisions exactly as it would for a changed text, and the response reports the destination without repeating the artifact beside it, exactly as for a run that changed something.

## The language of a report about the text

A run that reports on the text beside the text itself — the findings it carries forward, and which of them are unresolved — writes that report in the language of the Text Artifact rather than the language of the invocation, exactly as the no-change status above is written. So a Swedish artifact reviewed from an English-language invocation comes back with Swedish findings, whether the run corrected anything or was asked to correct nothing at all, and one text never produces a status in its own language beside a finding list in another.

Who reads it is what decides this. A report about a text is read by the reader of that text, who has to finish whatever the run left undone, and a report in whichever language the invocation happened to be written in reaches that reader in a language nothing about the text promised. The invocation's language is how the run was asked for; the artifact's language is what the run is about.

## The truth of a report about the text

Everything a run says about a text is true of the text it names. That holds for every statement the reply makes about a text, and not only for its findings and its account of the claims: a count, a length, a grammatical label, where a passage stands, and what a round did to a passage — moved it, removed it, replaced it, set a heading over it — each tells the reader something about the text they could check, and each is written so that the check holds.

A statement about the delivered text is checked against the delivered text after the last change to it, the closing mechanical pass included. Most of what a run knows about a text it learned while reviewing the text as it arrived, and the rounds changed that text afterwards, so a length measured before a round or a heading remembered from one describes a text the reader is no longer holding. Where a run measures a text with the Collection Library's measuring script, `scripts/article_anatomy.py`, a count or length the reply states is taken from that script's measurement of the text the statement is about, never from the run's own reading of it and never from a measurement of another state of the text. A statement about the text as it arrived says so, so that nobody reads it against the text delivered. A statement that cannot be made true of the text it names is left out.

The check is made on the reply as drafted, one statement at a time, once the text it describes is final, and each statement is read against the passage it names rather than against what the run remembers of it; a finding written during the review is checked in the same way against the text it was written about. A statement that something holds everywhere or nowhere — that a passage is unchanged, word for word what it was or untouched, that the rest of the text was left alone, that a name appears nowhere else, that a heading says nothing about its section — is checked against every part of the text it covers, because a single exception makes it false, and where there is one the statement names it or is narrowed to what holds. A statement of where wording came from, or of where a passage now stands, is checked by finding that passage in the text.

Who reads it decides this too. The reader of a report finds their way in the text by it, and a statement they check and find false costs them the trust they would have given every other statement in the same reply.

## Refusals

Every contradictory, meaningless, or unusable output request is refused before the first side effect. The cases this contract names are more than one Text Artifact where the Skill processes one, an output option together with In-place Editing, an output path equal to the input path, In-place Editing for inline text or a URL or an uploaded or read-only source, and a destination the run cannot write — a path whose parent directory does not exist among them.

Every such check that can be made by reading is made before anything is written, so a refusal leaves no partial effect behind: no file created, none truncated, none renamed, and no directory made. Where a conflict can only be discovered after a legitimate effect, the run stops there and reports the exact partial outcome rather than continuing.

A refusal follows the Collection's ordinary diagnostic and help conventions. It names what was wrong, prints the synopsis of the most specific recognized command page verbatim, and points at that command's own help form. An output option is refused rather than ignored where it has no work to do, a flag accepted and ignored teaching that flags sometimes do nothing.

# The correction brief

`<text>` is the current Text Artifact pasted whole — the text as it stands after every correction so far, never the text as it arrived and never an extract of it. `<findings>` is every finding of the most recent review, in the order it was recorded, each pasted whole under the same rule. `<genre>`, `<technique>` and `<language>` are the values the run resolved, written as the resources are named; write `none` for `<technique>` where no technique was resolved, and drop the sentence naming its resource with it. `<library>` is the Collection Library path this run resolved.

A brief-shortfall finding also carries its numbered requirement and exact, attributed supporting passages supplied by the parent review. Those are part of the finding, not an extra interpretation.

Tell the subagent nothing else. Not what an earlier round found, not what an earlier correction attempted, not which findings you think matter most, and not your reading of what the text is trying to do — that reading is the thing a fresh subagent is dispatched to be without.

Hand the filled-in brief to the subagent directly, as the whole of its instruction, and hand it over no other way. Never write it to a file and send a path in its place: this brief holds the user's text entire and every finding standing against it, and a file is a name some other process can read, replace, or delete for as long as the round lasts. A long text makes a long brief, and a long brief is passed whole anyway — trimming it, summarising it, and pointing at it are the three things this brief exists to rule out.

---

You are making one correction to one text. You have not seen this text before, and there is nothing you are expected to remember: the text below is its current state, and the findings below are the current review's, complete and as they were written. Repair them.

**The text.** This is the complete Text Artifact, exactly as it now stands:

`<text>`

**The findings.** This is every finding the review recorded against that text, complete and in the order it recorded them:

`<findings>`

**The contract.** The text is a `<genre>` in `<language>`, and it is held to `<technique>`. Read what it is held to before you change anything: `<library>/references/editorial/base.md` and `<library>/references/editorial/base.review.md`; `<library>/references/editorial/genres/<genre>.md` and the `.review.md` file beside it where one exists; `<library>/references/editorial/techniques/<technique>.md` and its `.review.md` the same way; `<library>/references/editorial/anti-slop.md`; and the `composition`, `review` and `anti-slop` scopes of the resolved language, which `uv run "<library>/scripts/languages.py" resolve --scope=composition --scope=review --scope=anti-slop "<language>"` returns. For `article`, `casestudy`, `column` and `opinion`, and for `webcopy`, also read `<library>/references/editorial/web-craft.md` and `<library>/references/editorial/web-craft.review.md`; for `article`, `casestudy`, `column` and `opinion` alone, also read `<library>/references/editorial/article-anatomy.md` and `<library>/references/editorial/article-anatomy.review.md`, which fix the parts, order and dimensions of such a text; and for those four and for `pressrelease`, also read `<library>/references/editorial/headlines.md` and `<library>/references/editorial/headlines.review.md`, which say how a headline and its subheadings are written. These are the only additional genre support files: follow no other genre links and load no unselected genre or technique. A review extension that is not there is not a defect. Run the resolver with `UV_NO_CACHE=1 UV_NO_PROJECT=1` and a fresh private `TMPDIR`, removing that directory afterwards, including on failure. Load no mechanics guidance and correct no spelling, punctuation, or grammar: a mechanical pass runs after you, and work you do there is work done twice.

**What you change, and what you preserve.** Repair what the findings name and nothing else. Every difference between the text you return and the text above is traced to a finding, or to what repairing a finding required, before this round is accepted, and a difference that traces to no finding is restored from the text you received — so a phrase you improved outside a finding is work that will be undone. Preserve everything the findings do not concern: every sentence, every fact, every quotation, every code sample, every heading, every piece of formatting and every line of frontmatter among them comes back exactly as you received it — a repair that improves a paragraph nobody complained about is a change nobody asked for and nobody will review. A code sample — a fenced block, an indented block, or an inline code span — is quoted material rather than the text's own prose: its contents are read past rather than read against the rules, so nothing inside one is a finding and nothing inside one is changed, the docstrings, comments, and string literals among them. Prose about code is ordinary prose and is read like every other sentence. Where a finding can be repaired several ways, make the smallest change that removes it. Where a finding names something you cannot repair without inventing a fact, changing what the text claims, or altering a quotation's meaning, stance, certainty or distinctive wording, leave that passage alone and say so: in an ordinary review this text is answerable to material you do not have, and a plausible invention is worse than an unrepaired finding. For a brief-shortfall finding carrying exact source support, use only that support or the text to supply what is missing. A repair never states the sender's message outright, since the message may always be conveyed indirectly. Source Fidelity binds the repair: retain attribution, uncertainty, scope, chronology, causality and quotation meaning. A requirement in the brief is not source evidence; where the finding has no support for a needed fact, source or quotation, leave it for the writer and report why.

**A defect of your own costs the whole round.** The review that follows you establishes whether this text has a defect it did not have when you received it — a headline or a heading claiming more than the text claims, a heading repeating the passage under it, a limit your repair dropped. Where it establishes one, the whole round is rejected: the text you received is restored entire, nothing you did survives however much else you repaired, and no fresh attempt follows. So a finding you cannot repair without creating another one is a finding you leave and say so, exactly as you would one you cannot repair without inventing a fact — an unrepaired finding a person can settle costs less than a repair that has to be thrown away with everything beside it.

**What a repair may take with it, and what it may not.** A finding names a defect, and what a repair removes is that defect. Where the defect a finding names is the whole of the passage — an opening that would sit in front of any text, a closing that restates what the reader has just read, a claim credited to nobody that the text cannot source — removing it may be the repair, and any claim removed with it must be named in your return. That stops at a sentence whose work is to bound what the text asserts — that something is not measured, not claimed, not witnessed or not general, or that the text is an observation of a document rather than a scene from an occasion. Remove or weaken one only where the finding names a defect inside the sentence, and only where a sentence you keep still states that limit in full, so the text bounds what it claims exactly as far as it did, or where the limit contradicts another passage of the same text. Otherwise leave it exactly as it stands and say so. Where the passage carries a claim beside the defect — a fact, an observation, the point the passage exists to make — the smallest change is the one that leaves that claim standing, and deleting the passage entire is not that change. And where you can see no way to remove the defect that does not take the claim with it, leave the passage alone and say so, exactly as you would a finding you cannot repair without inventing a fact: a person can give that claim what it needs or let it go, and a round that deletes it leaves them nothing to weigh. That judgement is about the passage in front of you and never about how much of the text is left — a short text is no licence to leave a finding standing, and a long one is no licence to go on cutting.

A repair at a punctuation joint can be the smallest change even when the finding names the implication created there rather than punctuation itself. In *We finished in March, the finance team got a new reporting tool the same month.*, the defect is the implication created by joining unrelated claims, not either claim. Repair it as *We finished in March. The finance team got a new reporting tool the same month.*: splitting at the joint removes the implication and keeps the reporting-tool fact. Do the same wherever the named defect is confined to a joint; do not delete either side or supply a relationship the text does not establish. This example does not admit a wider mechanics pass: it identifies the smallest repair for the finding already in hand.

Before you return the text, compare it before and after, claim by claim. Every claim you received must still appear with its scope, certainty, attribution, chronology, causality and meaning intact unless the finding named the whole claim as the defect; that exception does not reach a sentence whose work is to bound what the text asserts, which goes only on the two conditions above, and the number or concentration of findings changes nothing about that check. The concentrated anti-slop case makes the boundary visible: removing its patterns must not discard its claims about meeting load, documentation, decisions, satisfaction, distributed work, adoption conditions, or the synchronous/asynchronous trade-off. Repair the patterns around those claims. If one cannot be separated from its pattern, keep it and report the finding unresolved; never compress several content-bearing passages into a cleaner summary.

Where the text is an `article`, a `casestudy`, a `column` or an `opinion`, measure it before you return it: run `uv run "<library>/scripts/article_anatomy.py" -` with the complete corrected text on stdin, under the same `UV_NO_CACHE=1 UV_NO_PROJECT=1` and fresh private `TMPDIR` terms as the resolver above. Exit 0 settles the counted requirements only: it says they hold and nothing about the anatomy requirements the script does not count, so your return reports the text as conforming to the anatomy only where you examined every one of those too, and otherwise names the ones you did not examine. Exit 1 names each counted requirement of the article anatomy that fails, with the part, the rule and the figure measured: repair the ones a finding named and the ones your own repair introduced, then measure again, except a part a finding names as absent and a failure caused only by an absent part, which you leave unwritten and name in your return as left for a person to supply; a requirement the text was already failing when it reached you, and that no finding names, is left exactly as it stands like everything else the findings do not concern. Exit 2 says the script could not measure the text, and your return says so. Read every `heading_pairs` entry against the complete candidate and the loaded headline contract before returning, whatever the exit status: judge whether each part adds different information in different wording. Necessary repeated names and topic words can be legitimate, and a paraphrased echo can share no words; `shared_words` alone never authorizes a change or creates a finding. Verify absent or ambiguous sentence estimates against the text; on exit 2 inspect the pairs by hand. Repair echoes named by the findings or introduced by your own correction by wording the heading from its whole text or section without strengthening its claims and without pre-spending the judgement, figure or concession of a quotation standing under a subheading, then measure again. An unrelated pre-existing echo stays as received and is reported in your return, with the pair and reader loss; the evidence does not expand your correction authority. Report any echo you cannot repair within that authority the same way.

Where the text is a `pressrelease`, measure it before you return it the same way, with `--genre=pressrelease` before the `-`, which measures the two counted limits the genre states and nothing else of it. Exit 1 names the headline or the summary that is past its limit, with the rule and the figure measured: repair the ones a finding named and the ones your own repair introduced, then measure again, except a summary a finding names as absent, which you leave unwritten and name in your return as left for a person to supply; a limit the text was already failing when it reached you, and that no finding names, is left exactly as it stands. Exit 2 says the script found no level-1 heading or could not read the text, and your return says so. The output carries no heading pairs: read the headline and the summary against each other as the genre's review half says before returning.

**Your own working files.** Any file you write for your own working purposes — a candidate you measure, a draft you compare, anything you keep while you work — goes in a directory you created for this one round, under a name made unique when you created it, such as the one `mktemp -d` returns. Remove that directory before you return, including on failure. A fixed name under a shared temporary directory is not that directory, whether the directory is the system's own or a scratchpad your session was given: another run may be working at the same time, in the same place and on this same text, and write that same name. The file you come back to is then that run's work and not yours, and when you take it for your own stale copy and delete or replace it, you destroy work that is not yours, and nothing tells the run it came from.

**What you return.** The complete corrected text and a short note of which findings you repaired and which you left, with the reason for each you left. Where any repair removed a passage carrying a claim, name every removed claim and say which finding made the claim itself the defect, and name eve

1	# Delivery
2	
3	Every Skill that produces a Text Artifact delivers it the same way. This document is the complete contract: where a result goes, how a response carries the text, what the response carries when it went somewhere else, when a source file may be replaced instead, what happens when nothing changed, what language a run's own words about the text are written in and whether what those words say is true of the text they name, and what is refused before anything is written. It is a reference several Skills read rather than a runtime of its own. Each Skill exposes these rules through its own Formal Invocation and owns the names it gives them, so nothing here fixes how an option is spelled; what is fixed is the behaviour behind it.
4	
5	## The response is the default
6	
7	The default Output Target is the agent response. A run that keeps the default delivers the complete Text Artifact in the response and changes nothing on the filesystem: it creates no file, touches no file, and makes no directory. That includes scratch files and working copies of the artifact, wherever the Harness says temporary files belong.
8	
9	A Harness convention identifies where an authorized temporary file belongs; it does not authorize a write. If a run genuinely needs a scratch file while composing, it removes that file before delivery and restores the filesystem to the state in which it found it. Before reporting delivery, the run checks the filesystem locations it used, including the Harness scratch area, and never reports that nothing was written while a copy of the artifact remains on disk.
10	
11	An Output Target is independent of where the source material came from. Supplying a local file as source material selects no destination, and a run that reads a file still delivers to the response until the caller names somewhere else. Persisting a result is the caller's explicit choice, and making that choice is the whole of the authorization for it.
12	
13	## How a response carries the text
14	
15	A response carries a Text Artifact inside a fenced code block rather than as prose of the reply's own. A text and the words about it are two different things, and a reply that runs them together hands the reader a text nothing marks the edges of. Markdown is where that costs most: an artifact opening on a frontmatter delimiter, set directly beneath a paragraph the run wrote, turns that paragraph into a heading unless a blank line goes in between them — and a blank line there is what ends the frontmatter block the text was settled with. A fence removes the question rather than leaving each run to answer it, and the answers a run improvises are what made one saved reply in sixteen deliver a horizontal rule and a paragraph of configuration in place of a frontmatter block.
16	
17	The complete Text Artifact sits inside exactly one fenced code block, byte for byte as the run settled it: frontmatter, blank lines and trailing structure included. Nothing is added, dropped or re-wrapped between the fence lines, and one block rather than several, a text split across two fences being a text the reader has to reassemble.
18	
19	The fence is longer than the longest run of backticks inside the artifact, so a text carrying fenced code of its own cannot close it early. The info string names the text's format: `markdown` for a Markdown text, `html` for HTML, `text` for plain text.
20	
21	Everything the run says *about* the text sits outside the fence — the resolved configuration, the findings and which of them are unresolved, the claim account, where a technique came from, what the run could not do. Nothing of the run's own is inside it. What the run settled as part of the document does belong inside, the Handoff Metadata and any marking the user asked to have placed in the document itself among it, because that is the text as delivered rather than a remark about it.
22	
23	The rule reaches every complete text a reply carries, whether this contract calls that text delivered or not. A response-targeted run that changed nothing and has findings left fences the artifact like any other; a run that stopped before it could deliver and carries its preserved prose in the reply fences that prose, and says in its own words outside the fence what the prose has not been through. The short no-change status carries no text at all and so carries no fence. An explicit destination and In-place Editing receive the text itself and never a fence: a fence is how a reply holds a text apart from its own words, and a file has no words of its own to be held apart from.
24	
25	## An explicit destination
26	
27	An explicit destination is one filesystem path, and what exists at that path decides what happens to it.
28	
29	**A path that does not exist** creates exactly that one file and writes the complete Text Artifact into it. Exactly one file: nothing else is created beside it, and no directory is made to hold it.
30	
31	**A path naming an existing file** overwrites that exact file with the complete Text Artifact. No confirmation and no separate force option is required, and none is offered. Naming the path is the authorization, and demanding a second gesture on top of it would teach that naming a destination means something less than it says.
32	
33	**A path naming an existing directory** delivers into that directory under a filename the run derives, by the rules below. Choosing a directory selects a place, not a file, so it never overwrites a file already in it.
34	
35	## Deriving a filename for a directory
36	
37	A directory destination needs a name, and the name comes from what the run already knows. Take the first of these the run has: the basename of the local file that supplied the Text Artifact, the title of a referenced URL, then the Skill's own working title for the text it created. Reduce it to a name the filesystem accepts, and keep a suitable text extension — the source file's own where it had one, and otherwise the one matching the text's format.
38	
39	That gives a stem and an extension, and the stem stays as it is for every delivery into that directory. Where nothing exists at the derived name, that name is the file written. Where something exists there, the existing file is never overwritten: keep the original stem and take the first free numbered candidate in ascending order, beginning at `-2`. So `my-file.md`, `my-file-2.md`, `my-file-3.md` are one sequence, growing by one name at a time.
40	
41	A numbered candidate is never adopted as the new stem. A third delivery into a directory already holding the first two is `my-file-3.md` and never `my-file-2-2.md`, whose stem would fork the sequence in two and leave the directory recording how many times the same text arrived rather than which arrival it was. Ascending order with the first free name also means a number freed by a deleted file is used again before a higher one is taken.
42	
43	## What the response carries when a destination was named
44	
45	A run that delivers to an explicit destination does not repeat the Text Artifact in the response. The response says where the text went — the derived filename included, where the destination was a directory — and carries what the file cannot: the findings the run reports beside the text, and which of them are unresolved. Naming a destination is saying where the text goes, and printing it again spends output on what the caller is already holding, doubly so when the file just written holds it too.
46	
47	That holds whether or not the pass changed anything. A run that writes a file byte-identical to the source it read reports the destination and says the text needed no work, and does not become the one run that echoes a text the caller had before it started. The response is the default target precisely because a run that names no destination has nowhere else to put the artifact; naming one moves the text out of the response rather than duplicating it there.
48	
49	## In-place Editing
50	
51	In-place Editing replaces the single local file that supplied the Text Artifact with the result, instead of delivering it anywhere else. It is available only to a Skill whose work is to return a changed version of a text the caller already has.
52	
53	A Skill that creates a new Text Artifact never edits its own source material in place. The brief, the interview, the notes, and the article it draws on are where the text came from and not where it goes; a Skill that could overwrite them would make supplying a file a risk rather than a convenience, and would lose the material the result is answerable to.
54	
55	In-place Editing requires exactly one writable local source file, and it is mutually exclusive with a separate output option. A run replaces its source or delivers elsewhere, never both, and an invocation asking for both has named two destinations for one text.
56	
57	It is refused wherever there is no such file to replace. Text supplied inline in the invocation or taken from the conversation is not a file. 58	
59	An explicit output path equal to the input path is refused in favour of In-place Editing, and the refusal says which gesture to use. 60	
61	## When nothing changed
62	
63	A run may finish with nothing to change, and what it does then follows its destination.
64	
65	A response-targeted run that changed nothing returns a short no-change status in place of the text when no unresolved findings remain. When findings remain, deliver the complete Text Artifact in the response and report the unresolved findings separately.
66	
67	An in-place run that changed nothing leaves the source file untouched and returns the short status with any unresolved findings. Rewriting a file with its own contents would make its timestamp claim that something happened.
68	
69	That status is written in the language of the Text Artifact rather than the language of the invocation, so a Swedish text that needed no work is reported on in Swedish.
70	
71	An explicitly selected different file or directory still receives the complete Text Artifact when nothing changed. Creating that artifact is what was asked for, and a destination left empty because the text needed no work is a request refused without saying so. A directory destination derives its filename and resolves collisions exactly as it would for a changed text, and the response reports the destination without repeating the artifact beside it, exactly as for a run that changed something.

75	A run that reports on the text beside the text itself — the findings it carries forward, and which of them are unresolved — writes that report in the language of the Text Artifact rather than the language of the invocation, exactly as the no-change status above is written. 77	Who reads it is what decides this. The invocation's language is how the run was asked for; the artifact's language is what the run is about.
